utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-01-48-T, the Prosecutor versus Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are you ready to start?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'm ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Morrissey, your cross-examination, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Morrissey:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Zebic. Mr. Zebic, the first questions I have for you concern the structure of the civilian police services in Jablanica and Mostar. So these are going to be general questions that I have. First of all, the civilian police, of which you were a member, was administered under the Ministry of the Interior, the MUP; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your position was as the head of civilian police at the Jablanica police station; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Zebic, because in this court we have to deal with a number of acronyms for various departments of the government and the military, I'm going to ask you to explain a couple of the acronyms that are relevant to your part of the police force. Is the acronym for the Jablanica police station the SJB?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The literal translation of "SJB" would be "Stanica Javne Bezbjednosti," public security station. It includes the police station, as well as the police administration.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. And that police station has a local jurisdiction. And could you explain what that local jurisdiction was and what the limits of that jurisdiction were in area terms, please.

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Local jurisdiction implies that the law establishes that the public security station is territorially responsible for public security affairs within the confines of the municipality in which it was formed, meaning that all police matters and all administrative matters, such as the issuance of personal identity cards, driver's licences, and so on, is something that they would deal with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in peacetime and under normal circumstances, where did the responsibility for the Jablanica SJB end? If you were travelling down the highway to Mostar, the M17, how far did your jurisdiction reach and where did it stop?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The direction towards Mostar is to the south. It's some eight to nine kilometres. Topographically there is a bridge across the Neretva River at a place called Aleksin Han.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was it at that bridge that in normal circumstances the jurisdiction of your police station came to an end?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the other side of that bridge and proceeding southwards towards Dreznica and ultimately towards Mostar, in peacetime which police station normally had jurisdiction over that area?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Mostar Public Security Station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, I'm going to ask you in a moment about that -- that security station and how it fits into the hierarchy. But as a matter of realities, that M17 highway down to Mostar had been interrupted and cut off by HVO forces in August -- at least during the time of August and September of 1993. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps you're mistaken about the year. I think this was in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, no, I'm sorry, it may be that my question was misleading. The time period that I'm interested by is August and September of the year 1993. And what I wanted to ask you is not when the HVO first cut that road but as at August and September of 1993, was that road in fact cut? Had it already been cut by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to the south of Dreznica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. I understand. And as a result of that, was it your practice at the Jablanica SJB to assist with civilian police matters in Grabovica and the villages to the south of it, even though they were outside of your jurisdiction, simply because the Mostar police station was cut off from that area by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not the practice, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I've already asked you about what the SJB was, and now I have a question concerning the next level up the scale. Was there in Mostar a -- an institution called the Mostar CSB?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Could you just explain to the Tribunal here what is a CSB and how does it relate in the hierarchy to the SJB, and in particular how did the Mostar CSB relate to the Jablanica SJB.

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "CSB" means "Centar Sluzbi Bezbjednosti," public security centre, or security services centre. And it was part of the Ministry of the Internal Affairs, and it would unify a territory where there were several public security stations. The Mostar one would cover the public security stations in Jablanica, Konjic, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, just to clarify that a little bit further, was the Mostar CSB an institution that also contained the local police force centre for Mostar itself, as well as having these higher-level functions that you've mentioned?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question is not quite clear to me, but basically yes, the Security Services Centre would include all the public security stations in Mostar. At that point in time, unfortunately, Mostar was divided, so this Security Services Centre covered only the territory that was under the control of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. Very well. So in the administrative hierarchy of things, you, as the -- as the head of the SJB in Jablanica, in theory were under the jurisdiction higher up the chain of the Mostar CSB, and the Mostar CSB in turn was under the administration of the Ministry of the Interior, the MUP; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. I'm grateful to you for clarifying these matters. The minister in charge of the Ministry of the Interior at that time was a man named Bakir Alispahic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, I now want to turn in some more detail to the situation at Jablanica itself. At the Jablanica police station, you were the head of that police station and your deputy was Mr. Salihamidzic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I might -- just excuse me one moment, please, Mr. Zebic. Your Honours, just as a matter of caution, I think I should mention something now that that -- that name escaped my lips. The Prosecutors mentioned -- Yes, Your Honour, could we go to the private session, please. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Now we are in the open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Pardon me, Mr. Zebic, for that interruption. Your deputy was named Mr. Salihamidzic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And his nickname at the time was Cicko; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in August and September of 1993, there was another person present at the Jablanica SJB about whom I wish to ask you. Were you familiar with the -- an officer who was attached to the Mostar CSB named Sead Brankovic?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, was he an officer who was effectively employed by the Ministry of the Interior, rather than by the -- by the army or the Ministry of Defence? Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the information I had at the time, he was a member of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, a member of the public security.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. To your knowledge, did he report to persons at Mostar named Alica Bilic and Ramo Maslesa?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it's not quite clear to me now. You are mentioning two names now. Alica Bilic and Ramo Maslesa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry. Well, perhaps I should just ask you about that, bearing in mind that it's 11 years ago. Do you recall the name Ramo Maslesa?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ask do you recall that he was a senior officer at the Mostar CSB?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was my immediate superior.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And do you also recall Alica Bilic?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he was an officer of state security at -- at the Mostar CSB; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible. I'm not sure about that though. I cannot confirm it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's okay. I have to ask you the questions, but if you don't recall, then that's -- then that's your answer. May I come back to my original question: Was it your understanding that Sead Brankovic reported to these two individuals whilst he was placed at your police station in August and September of 1993?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. At all events, Sead Brankovic was not directly responsible or accountable to you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to your understanding, part of the reason why or a large part of the reason why Sead Brankovic was present at your police station is because of the disruption to communications between Mostar and the CSB in Mostar, on the one hand, and your police station in Jablanica, on the other hand; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's true that the roads were not clear. They were not passable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Very well. Now, I have some questions for you now about the military units that were in Jablanica. I bear in mind that you were -- you were employed by the Ministry of the Interior. But you may be able to answer these questions from personal knowledge. First of all, I've got some questions for you about the 44th Mountain Brigade. Now, was there a unit based at Jablanica which was a regular unit of the Bosnian army called the 44th Mountain Brigade?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it commanded by Enes Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at the time in August and September of 1993, was his deputy a man named Senad Dzino?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he have a military security officer named Zajko Sihirlic at that time?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you being a member of the -- of the civilian police, Zajko Sihirlic had no duty to report to you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, in fact, as you understood the procedures, his duties were, on the one hand, to his own commander, and, on the other hand, to report along the professional line up the scale of the SVB; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he did not report to the public security station, in any event.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. Now, I just have another question about the 44th Mountain Brigade. You -- you gave evidence yesterday, no doubt in completely good faith, that your recollection was that the 44th Brigade was in the zone of responsibility militarily speaking of the 4th Corps. Now, I have some questions for you about that. Were you aware that in July -- sorry, in June, actually, of -- of 1993 a new corps was brought into being, namely the 6th Corps, which assumed responsibility for some parts of the old 4th Corps's units?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that the 6th Corps had been formed, but the local brigade remained our local brigade, and I was -- continued to cooperate with them most frequently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that. In terms of your responsibilities, you -- you dealt with the 44th Brigade both before and after the creation of the 6th Corps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, in fact, the 44th Mountain Brigade had a -- very much a local character and had in its ranks very many local people; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Well, we've heard some sworn evidence in this court from other witnesses that the 44th Brigade came to be under the control directly of the 6th Corps. I take it you don't dispute that that is what happened after the 6th Corps was created in June of 1993.

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are military matters, and I don't really have much interest for them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. Well, I understand that it was not a matter that impacted on your operations to any significant extent. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... All right. Now, you've indicated that there were daily meetings held at your police station at which various policemen attended. Was it the practice that you would invite a representative from the 44th Brigade to be present at those meetings in order to liaise properly and in order not to cause trouble for the military and for them not to cause trouble with you?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did have such meetings, not on a daily basis though. Sometimes it happened at the public security station, and sometimes they were held at the 44th Brigade command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And who was the 44th Brigade person whom you dealt with most frequently in terms of that liaison?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly the commander of the military police company and this person whom you mentioned who was in charge of security, Mr. Sihirlic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And just so that the record reflects this, you've indicated the commander of the military police. By that do you mean Mr. Sead Kurt?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. All right. Now -- and thank you once again for clarifying these -- these organisational matters. There's one other matter I want to clarify with you again, and that was the -- just the structure of the War Presidency. The War Presidency was a -- a civil authority headed by Dr. Safet Cibo, C-i-b-o; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it had responsibility for logistics and -- and for effectively civil administration in the Jablanica area at that time?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You as civilian chief -- sorry, civilian police chief were an ex officio member of that War Presidency; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Yes, I think that's the institutional questions. Now, could I just ask you some questions about early September 1993 and the situation that existed in Jablanica at that time. First of all, Jablanica was a -- a small town -- well, perhaps could you tell us what was the normal peacetime population of Jablanica before hostilities broke out?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were around 12.600 people living in the entire territory of the municipality of Jablanica. Over 70 per cent were Bosniak. Around 20 per cent were Croats. And the rest were Serbs and others, such as gypsies, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So predominantly -- predominantly Bosniak but with significant populations of -- with a significant population of Croats and -- and also other populations present; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The township of Jablanica itself, what was the population of that township before hostilities began? Approximately.

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three, four thousand. Three and a half, four thousand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. After hostilities commenced between the HVO and the Bosnian government army, did Jablanica come under fire on any occasions?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the outbreak of the conflict between the army and the HVO, Jablanica was never under attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, well, perhaps my question wasn't clear. I'm really asking about the time after that -- that conflict broke out. Once it broke out, did Jablanica then come to be under fire?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Beginning with April 1992 until then, there were frequent shellings of the population centre of Jablanica itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned the year 1992, Mr. Zebic. It's -- it's -- is it your understanding that the conflict between the HVO and the -- and the Bosnian government army commenced with hostilities at Prozor late in 1992?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I misspoke. I'm sorry, Your Honours. It should be April 1993. That's when the hostilities began around Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you've indicated that after that time, Jablanica did come under shelling. Do you -- are you -- do you mean artillery fire from the HVO side?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, only.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And did that shelling continue throughout 1993? I'm particularly thinking about August and September of 1993 when I ask question.

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be certain about these two months, but I believe in that period there was constant fire around Jablanica and on Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in terms of the fire on Jablanica, did that cause casualties among the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a hospital in Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it set up to deal with the volume of injuries and wounds and disasters which occurred once the shelling began in Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not a medical professional. All I can say is that many, many wounded people, fighting men and civilians were taken care of by that hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall how many doctors they had on the staff there, from your own knowledge?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly, but I know some doctors from Mostar had come to help out at the Jablanica hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it they were pretty busy, from what you were able to observe. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, every day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And another effect of the HVO conflict was that transport to Konjic became quite difficult; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And although you've answered this question in another form already, transport to Mostar became quite difficult; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was almost impossible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I have some brief questions now, turning away from Jablanica to Mostar, about your understanding of the situation in Mostar. It was well known by August and September of 1993 that the extreme elements of the HVO had declared their intention to make Mostar the capital city of the new Republic of Herceg-Bosna; is that true?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to confirm, but facts seem to support what you just said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you, as police chief, came to know that a large number of persons were arriving on Bosnian government territory from territory owned or held by the HVO; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the translations that we have, various terms are used, and I wanted to ask you about those terms. We have the term "refugee" in some papers and also the term "expellee" and a variety of different terms are used. What was your understanding of where these people were coming from, the people who arrived on your territory? Were they coming from villages from which they were expelled, or were they coming from prison camps, or are there other sources as well?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Among civilians who arrived in the territory of Jablanica, there were many who had been in prison camps in Herzegovina. Some had been expelled from villages in Eastern Herzegovina, Gacko, Nevesinje, Stolac, for example. But in the period that we are discussing now, the summer of 1993, people were coming mainly from camps, locals of Capljina, Stolac, Mostar, that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. Now, is it accurate to say that by the end of -- or sorry, perhaps I should ask this: Throughout summer, throughout the summer of 1993, there was a -- a fairly steady stream of refugees and expellees coming onto the territory under the jurisdiction of your police station; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you put them to live, and how did you find places for them to live?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people who were directly involved in finding accommodation for those people would be better placed to tell you, such as members of the Civilian Defence Staff, members of the Red Cross. But from what I know, at one point there were many more refugees and people who had been expelled in Jablanica than locals, and it was very difficult - you're right about that - to put them up in the small area of our town, squeezed as it was between two enemy armies. They were put up in schoolhouses, in cinema halls, in museums even, in private family houses, in office space of various enterprises, some prefab buildings that had been left over on various construction sites. The problem was really severe in a small township like Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it accurate to say that the problem spilled over into other villages in the area? I'm thinking now of Grabovica, Buturovic Polje as examples.

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll come to the Grabovica situation in detail soon. But apart from Buturovic Polje, can you comment on any other places that you now recall refugees being sent in order to accommodate them?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you one thing. You're probably not very familiar with the situation there. Konjic was under fire. You couldn't send them to Mostar. In the west, there was the HVO, which wouldn't allow any communication. So we couldn't send them on anywhere. We had to let them stay where they were, in our town, and find a place for them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. And I take it from what you say that at the end of -- at the end of August and early in September the problem didn't stop but, rather, it got worse and more refugees just kept coming. Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just had a couple of specific questions about places where refugees were -- were housed. First of all, I take it it was not the job of you or your police force directly to -- to house these people but it was the job of other civilian authorities. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, was there still in existence the old -- an old quasi-military organisation called the TO?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time you mean? In 1993?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And I mean specifically end of -- end of September and -- sorry. Pardon me. I take that back. I mean specifically end of August and early September 1993. Did the TO still exist at that time or had it been abolished already?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be sure about this. If it existed, it was just the local command in charge of dealing with local problems of Jablanica --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- only.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. And in terms of providing security at various important civil institutions, was that the role of the TO, to provide, for example, guards at the hydroelectric plant and so on?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. The police didn't do this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I understand. I've got some questions about one particular institution; that's the museum in Jablanica. Now, to your knowledge, was the museum a public building which had to be used because there was nowhere else to put certain refugees?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the answer. Could the witness be asked to speak up a little.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zebic, the interpreter just had difficulty hearing your answer. Then although -- actually, I heard it. But would you mind just repeating it, please, for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sometimes we need to speak a little bit clearly for the interpreter's benefit here. Very well. Now, can you just explain how big that museum was -- sorry, that's a meaningless question. I'll take that back. I'll deal with it another way. At the end of August of 1993, to the best of your recollection, how many -- how many of the Bosniak refugees were to be found at the museum?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly above 100. I can't be sure about the number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now, Mr. Zebic, I take it that -- I'll put this in very general terms first and I'll come to specifics in a minute. These were very challenging and difficult times for a policeman to be doing his work; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was a time of some social dislocation with tensions between parts of the community that lived in Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those tensions were magnified and complicated by the arrival of traumatised, hungry, and unhappy Bosniaks from the HVO territories or HVO-held territories; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it was also a time during which local criminals found it easier than usual to procure guns and weapons; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the police therefore had a full-time job in preserving public order in Jablanica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And furthermore, I take it that you were not able to double your -- sorry, I'll ask the question another way. Resources, as far as manpower goes, were quite scarce for the police because the army was making demands on the young men in the territory; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a fact that the army had priority. However, the police was also assisted by a number of reserve policemen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. How many regular police were stationed at the -- at the Jablanica police station?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In wartime conditions, everybody is in regular service. I mentioned the reserve only because at the beginning of the conflict a number of those reservists were deployed in the police station of Jablanica, because that's where they had their wartime assignment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. So what were the numbers of -- of participating police at the Jablanica police station?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It varied from 150 to 200.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those 150 to 200 had the tasks of doing all police work within your -- within your municipality; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. The military police in Jablanica, to your knowledge, were commanded by Sead Kurt; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only the military police of the 44th Mountain Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. Now, as far -- I understand you weren't in command of them, but I just want you to assist the Tribunal to know what sort of tasks they had to perform. Was one task that you knew the military police to perform to protect the command post of the 44th Mountain Brigade and provide security for that important institution?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not up to me to judge really. I think you should ask a military expert.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're going to, but we'd value what you saw as well because you were there. I appreciate that you -- you weren't in command of these people. Are you able to comment on this: At the museum facility, so far as you understood, was the security there provided by the military police from the 44th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, at that museum the military police had its offices, its own space, and it's possible that military police would normally be seen around and in that building at that time, but I don't believe they were serving as guards at the museum where displaced and other persons who had come because they had been expelled were put up temporarily.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now, I want to turn to the village of Grabovica and your knowledge of that, even though it was outside of your jurisdictional area, on your evidence. You knew that the village of Grabovica had ethnic Croats in it on both sides of the river; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You knew that as time went by refugees were located with those villagers to a large extent on the left bank but also on the right bank to some degree; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You knew that a unit called Cedo's Wolves or sometimes, I think, called the Igman Wolves were billeted in -- in some business offices of the hydroelectric plant amongst the houses on the left bank; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the left bank, yes, but there were no houses around, I must say. The houses of local people were slightly further below the offices that you mention.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You knew that a unit called the Handzar Division, a small unit called the Handzar Division, came to be located in the village of Grabovica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Did you ever meet a man -- an Albanian man, the commander of a unit called Handzar, who went by the name of Dzeki, D-z-e-k-i?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about him. For a while, they were in the town of Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. You knew that Zuka's unit, under the direction of Zulfikar Alispago, was based at Donja Jablanica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll come back to some of these questions in a moment. I've just got some general questions about that. To your understanding, the policy of the Bosnian government during the war was to fight to preserve a multi-ethnic community; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, in fact, as far as you're concerned, the killings that happened in Grabovica caused you major difficulties with the civilian population at a later time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as you could see, the killings that took place in Grabovica were totally contrary to the aims of the Bosnian state; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, returning to the relations between the army and the citizens of Grabovica before the killings took place. You were aware that the army had attempted to establish good relations with those citizens; is that correct? Providing medical facilities and so on.

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. For the most part, it was provided all from Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, it was just -- maybe you can clarify this, but -- I think you already have clarified it. Thanks. All right. And did you yourself have occasion to visit the village of Grabovica in the weeks or so before the killing took place?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, then I had a series of questions, but I won't ask you those questions, since you didn't go there. Very well. I want to move forward now to approximately the 6th of -- of September. So now I'm going to ask you some questions about the -- the events that you were involved in. On or about the 6th of September, did Minister Bakir Alispahic pass through the village -- sorry, the town of Jablanica on his way down to Mostar?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when he -- while he was passing through, did he attend -- to your knowledge, did he attend a meeting of commanders -- or perhaps I shouldn't use the word "commanders." Did he attend a meeting of -- of military leaders in the town of Jablanica? I'm not suggesting that you attended, but to your knowledge, did he attend such a meeting?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On his way down to Mostar, was he accompanied by a unit of the Ministry of the Interior sometimes known -- or known as the Laste Unit?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you told us yesterday that the Laste Unit was en route to help at the Mostar CSB, and that was a truthful and accurate answer, wasn't it, that you gave yesterday?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did that Laste Unit stop in Jablanica for a night, or did it just pass straight on through to Mostar, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that now. It's possible that they did spend the night, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Okay. Now, you indicated yesterday to my learned friend Mr. Sachdeva that you knew because of your contacts at the 44th Mountain Brigade that Sarajevo units were being billeted in the village of Grabovica. And my question for you is: Did you know on the night of the 8th and the 9th - that's the night beginning -- the end of the 8th and the morning of the 9th, that night - did you know that a new group of refugees from the Dretelj camp came up the road from Dreznica, coming to Grabovica, and some of them ultimately coming to -- to Jablanica? Was that something within your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that at the moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Just excuse me one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, the -- Excuse me, please, Mr. Zebic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry to say that I -- there's a document I wish to show the witness but it's been tendered into evidence but I don't have the number. I have the Defence number. If I provide the Defence 65 ter number, it may be that I can be assisted by the court staff. And I apologise for not having the proper number. The Defence document is D623A. It was tendered, I believe, through the witness Salko Gusic, and it's a document from Mr. Sihirlic addressed to the 6th Corps command and it concerns the movement of those people up the road and other things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I'm going to show you now, Mr. Zebic, is an order. You may not have seen it. And I wouldn't have naturally come to you. But it's now in evidence in this case, and I just want you to look at it and tell me if you have seen it and then I'll ask you some questions in any event about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I believe it to be 623A.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: -- just inquire from my learned friend, does he mean 623B?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, I -- the Defence counsel is happy to say that I'm not sure which one I'm referring to. I believe I'm referring to 623. I apologise for this. It's a -- it's a record-keeping glitch, and I rely very heavily on Mr. Cengic in these situations, and he's -- he's not able to be here. I think I can deal with the matter a different way. Perhaps if I can just --

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If I may be of assistance, I think it is 623B.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think 623B just appeared on the screen, and that certainly is the one that we want.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Defence Exhibit D153.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm grateful to the court staff, D153.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'm grateful to the Prosecutor for assisting on that occasion. This is -- what I'm showing you now is a military document, and I'm not sure whether you've seen it before, but I would just ask you to briefly look at it and see whether you have seen it before and ...

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I don't think it's fair to leave it in front of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: In those circumstances, I've had ask that that be withdrawn from in front of him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Okay, Mr. Zebic. I won't ask you about that document. Did you become aware on the morning of the 9th, that is to say, before you were told of the killings or any of the trouble that happened, did you become aware that a new group of refugees had come up the highway via Grabovica, some of whom arrived in -- in Jablanica that night or early in the morning of the 9th?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember. Unless there was some security problems, I didn't even have to know that that morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. Okay. All right. Now, finally, before we get to the -- the episode of the -- of your involvement in these sad events: You've indicated that you came to know that there was a -- a forward command post, also called an IKM, in Jablanica via your contacts in the 44th Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Amongst other things, with the 44th Brigade and also the command. I think a lot of the citizens in Jablanica knew that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. The fact is Mr. Halilovic was a very famous person in -- in Bosnia at that time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, he was the -- the person who had founded the army and -- or at least presided over the -- the creation of the Bosnian army as a viable fighting force; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At one stage, did his picture hang in the -- in the Jablanica police station?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did an order come to take it down?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no order to put the photograph up or to take it down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know that there was an inspection team of the Supreme Command Staff in the area of Herzegovina and specifically in Jablanica headed by Sefer Halilovic and also including other well-known generals: Vehbija Karic, Zicro Suljevic, and Rifat Bilajac?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that these names that you just mentioned were talked about, but I'm not aware of the context in which the names were mentioned because these names were that well known to me that I knew that we were talk about senior-ranking officers of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. And just -- I want to ask you this: In -- in late August and early September of 1993, did you personally meet Sefer Halilovic in that time?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you speak to him on the telephone?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any other form of communication with him directly in that time?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. All right. Now, I want to turn to the morning of the 9th -- sorry, well, the day of the 9th of September, when your involvement in this matter effectively commenced. You indicated that you spoke to Mr. Salihamidzic and that you had a discussion with him about what to do when you received the bad news, or the first rumours of bad news. Now, you were shown yesterday a document by my learned friend the Prosecutor Mr. Sachdeva, which was a note by -- by Mr. Salihamidzic concerning his activities. And I just wanted to ask you this: He says in that note that at 1500 hours he set off to go out onto the terrain to have a look to see what had happened. And what I want to put to you is this: That document was written at the time and that accurately reflects the time which he set off; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I just want to ask you a little bit about what happened before he left and about the news that you had available to you in that time. You've already indicated how it was that you spoke to Mr. Salihamidzic. You had a discussion with him about your jurisdiction and your powers to act; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was a real issue because in theory your powers ended at the Aleksin Han bridge; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, again, this is purely in theory: In theory, it should have been the Mostar police station that looked after any crimes, and of course leaving aside the issue of whether the military join in. But in terms of jurisdiction, from your point of view, if it was a police matter, in theory it should have been a Mostar police matter; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as well as that jurisdictional issue, from the news you had, there was the possibility that military personnel might have been involved in the crimes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And it was for that reason essentially that you called Sead Kurt to have a discussion with him.

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That and the other reason is that the military component did have the option of going to that area legally and then we could go with them in order to assist them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And when you say they could go there legally, that's because that village was, from a military point of view, within the zone of operations of the 44th Brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But that was your thinking at the time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. And you'd been dealing with the 44th Brigade in detail for many months, and indeed you kept dealing with them after that for -- for months as well; is that true?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just in terms of that issue of -- of the 44th Brigade, did you ever meet with the commander of the 6th Corps, Salko Gusic?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever meet with the head of military security of the 6th Corps, a man named Nermin Eminovic?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps we saw each other, but I didn't record that meeting anywhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall any such meeting yourself, regardless of notes?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And finally, did you yourself have any -- I'm jumping forward a little bit now, but -- well, I may be jumping forward. I'll ask you the question, and then you can tell me if I am or not. In -- in September of 1993, did you have any personal contact yourself with Jusuf Jasarevic, who was the head of military security within the Bosnian army?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you send any reports or communications to Jusuf Jasarevic yourself during that time?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And indeed, you had no obligation to send any such reports to Mr. Jasarevic, because he was head of military security and you were in the -- in the MUP; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks. And just one other background matter which I forgot to ask you earlier: You personally were not included in any way in any discussions about military operations that were to take place early in the September 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks. Very well. Now, I want to turn to -- we'll come back to your investigations here. You've indicated that you -- you made contact with Mr. Kurt, and then at 1500 hours it's the fact that Salihamidzic left. Could I ask you the question: What vehicle did Salihamidzic and Kurt leave in? Was it a military vehicle or a -- a MUP vehicle?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've indicated that to the best of your recollection that they returned two to three hours later. But can I suggest to you that they returned at approximately 6.00, maybe a tiny bit before 6.00? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall whether it was dark or getting dark at the time when they returned?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was still visible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. It may be stretching your memory. I'm just asking you to extend your memory the best you can. Had it started to get dark at that point, or was it still fully daylight, or can you simply not remember that much detail?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember everything, but since it was still September, it's possible that it was still visible at around 1800 hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall whether or not when Mr. Salihamidzic and Mr. Kurt came back they had with them any elderly people who they'd picked up on the road?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My deputy came to see me, so I don't know who they came back with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I take it you didn't see them arrive back. Is that the situation?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, is it the appropriate time for us to take a break?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll have a break and we'll resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you again, Mr. Zebic. Before we broke, I was asking you questions about what happened before Mr. Salihamidzic left, and now I want to turn to what happened when he came back. He came back, and you had a discussion with him. And could I ask you, did -- I'm not suggesting that you should have done this, but can I just ask: Did you in fact take any notes of the conversation that you had with him on that occasion, when he arrived back?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry, both Mr. Halilovic and I couldn't hear the answers there. I apologise, Mr. Zebic. I should indicate, if it's a technological problem, I can hear my own voice as barristers can. I'll attempt to proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to hear me, Mr. Zebic?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can hear you now, but I couldn't hear you before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. I'll just ask you the question again that I had. Did you -- did you take any notes of that discussion that you had with Mr. Salihamidzic when he first arrived back or not?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Anyway, you've read the report that Mr. Salihamidzic ultimately wrote. And I take it what he told you when he came back was essentially the information that he had up to that point; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he told you about going to the village and meeting with Mr. Solakovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he told you about the rumours that he heard? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he told you about going to look to see if he could see a body down by the Neretva River which was rumoured to be there but that he hadn't been able to see any such body; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He told you that while he was doing that, Sead Kurt had been approached - and this is all on the afternoon of the 9th of September - Sead Kurt had been approached by Ramiz Delalic, Celo, and spoken to while up on the bridge; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Next to the bridge, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Pardon me. I accept the correction. And did he tell you whether or not he had encountered any civilians on the way back to Jablanica and given any such civilians a ride or any assistance?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, now, I just want to ask you some questions about your state of knowledge at that stage. Once you've spoken to Salihamidzic, you knew that there had probably -- very probably been murders committed in -- in Grabovica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you knew it was necessary to take measures to evacuate some civilians; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You knew that a local commander there -- well, sorry, I shouldn't say "local" because he was from Sarajevo -- but a particular commander in Grabovica, namely, Adnan Solakovic, was expressing fears for the safety of his own troops; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what my deputy told me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I understand you -- you're going on what you were told here by your deputy. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But your information was also that Ramiz Delalic, Celo, was present in Grabovica and that he was not cooperative or friendly to the police when he met -- to the military police when he met them next to the bridge; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judging by his reactions, that was my conclusion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. And it was your opinion at that stage that it would be dangerous to go onto the terrain in Grabovica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But even so, you realised that there still had to be an effort made to -- to evacuate civilians, and you began to take steps to do that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in -- in doing that, you made contact with the leader of the Zulfikar unit, Zulfikar Alispago; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I informed the War Presidency first.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. I'll come to the War Presidency discussion in a minute. I just want to deal with the -- the contacts with -- with Zulfikar Alispago. Because he's called "Zuka" in many people's language, that's how I -- did you know him as "Zuka"?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And if I refer to him as "Zuka," you'll know who we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Was it you personally who contacted Zuka in order to help evacuate the civilians, or did you -- was that done by Salihamidzic or -- or another person?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was Salihamidzic with the son-in-law of one of the civilians from Grabovica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And again, jumping forward slightly, is it your understanding that that son-in-law ultimately drove to Grabovica with Zuka and rescued two Croat civilians from the right bank a bit later that evening?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. Now, was an operation -- I shouldn't -- well, I've used the term "operation." Perhaps I shouldn't in the context of this case. I'll -- were arrangements then made to get vehicles to drive down to -- to Grabovica and bring away elderly Croat civilians who were there?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But this was done because the War Presidency organised it as well as other civilian bodies in Grabovica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it still was the fact, wasn't it, that Zulfikar Alispago cooperated in that venture and assisted with the removal of elderly Croats from Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, as a policeman who's been in -- in action for a number of years, would you agree with this proposition: That any investigation of a crime starts off with acquiring information about that crime? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the fact is at this stage you had some information but not enough for you to be comfortable about what had happened in Grabovica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you also knew that it may well happen that the SVB, the military security service, would be involved in investigating this -- these killings because it could be that military persons were among the killers, and that was your state of mind even from the very beginning; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was in their jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Now, we've -- did you ever encounter -- would you just excuse me a moment, Mr. Zebic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Would Your Honours just excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I just want to put something from a couple of witnesses whose names I think -- identities may have been suppressed. Could we go into the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, just -- the reason we've done that: I just want to put a couple of persons' names to you. Do you know a woman from the left bank of -- of Grabovica called Katica Miletic?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps Ms. Miletic -- was not actually protected. Perhaps this part can be placed into open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll lift that part. You may proceed, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Zebic, and I suppose -- at that time, you were aware of the potential bad feeling of newly arrived refugees towards the local Croat population in the municipality of -- of Jablanica generally speaking; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And with respect to the killings that -- that you were now hearing about for the first time, you had to deal with the operative possibility that some of these refugees might have played a part in the killings; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I didn't think any of the refugees could have done it. It didn't occur to me at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did it occur to you at a later time that perhaps some such refugees may have been involved in the killings?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had absolutely no indications to suggest that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. But -- no, I understand your position is that it was a military police investigation in any event, but although you didn't have any specific indications, wasn't it something that you turned your mind to as an experienced policeman, bearing in mind the possible ill will between the new arrivals and the existing Croat population?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought it could be among the population. There was a certain degree of ill will when those civilians arrived in Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But I take it from your answers that -- well, you tell me if I'm right about this, but your -- your previous experience of Grabovica was that it was pretty peaceful; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, the situation in Grabovica was significantly more peaceful than the situation in Jablanica, as far as relations between Croats and Muslims went; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, did you have any personal involvement in finding a place for these -- for the rescued Croatians at Jablanica, or did that job fall to somebody else to arrange?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the job to -- of the Red Cross in Jablanica and the Civil Defence Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand, therefore, that it fell outside of your direct function. Could you just exercise your memory and see whether you remember actually seeing any of these people arriving in -- in Jablanica around that time.

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Very well. Now, I'd moved ahead of something there, but you mentioned that you -- that you went to the War Presidency. I take it the order of things was this: That you arrived -- that Salihamidzic came back somewhere approaching 1800 hours; that you then spoke to him for a period of time; and that you then went to the War Presidency. And what I want to ask you is: How long did you speak to Mr. Salihamidzic? Was it an hour? Was it three-quarters of an hour? Was it half an hour? Or what figure, to the best of your memory, did you spend speaking to him?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a brief conversation. He just told me about what had happened, from what he had heard, and he said that in agreement with Mr. Solakovic the civilians should be pulled out of Grabovica. It took no more than ten minutes, and after that I went to the Presidency with my deputy to inform them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And how long did it take you to get over to the Presidency? Was that a one-minute walk or a ten-minute walk?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three minutes' walk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I take it you had the opportunity to speak fairly swiftly to Dr. Cibo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you spent some time explaining to him what had happened; is that correct? Or perhaps you could tell us, how long did you spend telling him what happened?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe the same time it took me to discuss it with my own deputy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Look, I understand these are estimates, but -- now, as soon as Mr. Salihamidzic came back, you knew that it was a matter of significant urgency to deal with the -- with the refugee situation. Was a contact made with Zulfikar Alispago before you spoke to Dr. Cibo or afterwards? Or both?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I failed to mention that it was my deputy who contacted Mr. Alispago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, okay. Well, thank you for clarifying that. But just in terms of the visit to Dr. Cibo, did -- was contact made with Zulfikar before you went -- before you spoke to Cibo or after you spoke to Cibo or both before and after?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never had any contact with Mr. Alispago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, no, but when your deputy Salihamidzic made contact with Zuka, did he do that before your meeting with Cibo or after it or both, before and after?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it happened this way: I'm not speaking with absolute certainty, but Mr. Salihamidzic contacted the brother-in-law -- the son-in-law of those two elderly people from Grabovica, and then he asked Mr. Alispago to save, to rescue the parents of his wife from Grabovica. Maybe it wasn't even my deputy who talked to Alispago. Maybe it was the son-in-law of those civilians in Grabovica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, it may be that you're correct about that, and obviously there was a contact between this civilian and Zulfikar Alispago. But I take it that there -- I mean, there must have been - and I put to you there that is there was a contact directly between yourself, either you or your deputy, on the one hand, and Alispago, on the other hand, with the purpose of arranging the -- the evacuation. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. So I take it -- I've been -- I've been showering you with questions on this topic, I know. But is the position this: You really can't recall precisely when it was that contact occurred between the police, on the one hand, and Zulfikar Alispago, on the other hand, relative to the meeting with Dr. Cibo? Is that a fair comment? You just can't quite remember what the order of it was?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall. That's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Putting all these things together, if the -- if the -- if Salihamidzic came back at around 6.00 and if the time periods are as you've described, what you'd say is, I take it, that contact was made by Dr. Cibo at the War Presidency in that phone call you described to the IKM at approximately half past 6.00 or maybe a bit before that time. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Just in terms of the phone call made by Dr. Cibo, can you recall - tell us if you can recall - whether it was dark or light outside at the time when that call was made.

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Very well. Now, the next thing you gave evidence about happening was the arrival of -- of the Minister of the Interior, Mr. Bakir Alispahic. And I just want to ask you that -- about this. In the time after you spoke to Dr. Cibo and after he spoke to the IKM, as you've described, you, I take it, were then concerned with matters arising out of this bad news that you'd received; namely, helping the civilians who had to be rescued. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not only my concern. That's why I went to the War Presidency, to inform them about this entire event.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I understand, it had to be a joint effort. But that was the -- I mean, that was the thing you were working on in that hour after you'd been to see Dr. Cibo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was summoned by the War Presidency. More precisely, and I was told that a minister had come to my office to see me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you when you got that summons?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. So the situation is that you were at the War Presidency involving yourself in -- in helping those who had to be evacuated and someone from the War Presidency then gave you the news that a minister had arrived; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I did not get interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I indicate I didn't hear any translation of that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter's apology. I didn't turn on the microphone. Could -- I can repeat the whole answer. The minister was on his way and the passage was very difficult through the mountains.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time were you told that the minister was on his way? What time did that piece of news reach you?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could have been around 7.00 p.m., maybe past 7.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And who was it who told you that piece of news?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The clerk on duty at the police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And did that clerk on duty telephone you while you were at the War Presidency to give you that information?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And did the intended route of Minister Alispahic take him through the village of Grabovica or not?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was not able to go through Grabovica. In order to reach Jablanica, he had to cross the mountain around Jablanica. He had to go through Glogosnica and from there, there was transportation available to go to Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. And where was it proposed that you would meet the minister?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the public security station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it expressed to you that the minister was already aware of the killings at Grabovica or not?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why was he coming to see you?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He decided so. He's senior in rank. It was up to him to decide.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I understand he had the competence to make that decision, but my question is: To your knowledge, why did he make that decision? Why did he come to Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had to go through Jablanica in order to return to Sarajevo. He was on his way back to Mostar, so he had to pass through Jablanica anyway to go to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he accompanied by any of the Laste Unit on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you at that time whether or not Sefer Halilovic was under surveillance by members of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you whether Sefer Halilovic's telephone calls were being intercepted by the MUP?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you whether there were operative measures of any sort in place by the MUP against Sefer Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you spoke to him, did he have any familiarity with these killings, as far as you could see, or was it you who broke the news to him about what had happened?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I was the first to tell him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And how long did it take you to explain what you knew?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And after that, you've indicated that -- that you arranged a telephone call to be placed from your institution over to the -- to the IKM; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did this call take place from the War Presidency or from the police station to the IKM?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the public security station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
