utterances.text: And I just have to ask you this question, Mr. Zebic: You indicated in evidence here that you'd -- you hadn't yourself spoken to Halilovic or had any contact with Halilovic, and my question is: Have you ever told anyone that you did speak to Sefer Halilovic in this time?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this telephone conversation that you've given evidence about you've indicated lasted no more than two to three minutes; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that phone call, according to your recollection, commenced with Mr. Alispahic saying the word "Sefer"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And most of the rest of the telephone call, the rest of that two- to three-minute period consisted of Mr. Alispahic relaying down the telephone the news that you'd already told him; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did not hear the voice on the other end yourself in any way; correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And apart from saying the word "Sefer" when he commenced the phone call, this -- Mr. Alispahic didn't use the word "Sefer" again during that telephone call, did he?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after the telephone call, he didn't mention Sefer again by name but he just told you, I suggest, "You help the military security out when they investigate"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sounds about right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And after that telephone call, did you tell any other person about this telephone call? Did you mention it to any other person?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote that down in a document that I drafted and sent to the ministry several days later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you tell -- the question was though not whether you wrote it down, but did you tell somebody? And I suppose I'll focus the question this way: Did you tell Mr. Salihamidzic either that night or the following morning that you had been present at that telephone call?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. All right. Can you remember where it was that you told that to Mr. Salihamidzic? Can you remember where that conversation took place?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember that specific time, but every day and most of the time we talked in my office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, I just want to put a couple of propositions about Mr. Alispahic's movements. I put it to you that at that time when he came to Jablanica he expressed to you that he was on his way to Konjic because he had a meeting concerning munitions and -- and in particular a munitions factory the following day with another minister, named Rusmir Mahmutcehajic.

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe he did continue his trip.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But what I'm asking you is did -- well, I didn't ask you this before. I'll now ask you it. Did he tell you that, that he was going on to see Rusmir Mahmutcehajic, Sefer Halilovic, Vehbija Karic, and others in order to discussion munitions and in particular a particular munitions plant at Konjic? Did he give you that information?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I really don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's okay. Perhaps I could ask you this question. This might assist. Did he tell you he was going to meet Sefer Halilovic the following day in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. All right. Thank you for that. Now, I want to take you to the following day. We've now finished with the 9th, the activities on the 9th of September, and we'll move to the 10th of September. Now, on that day, you believed that everyone who needed to be evacuated had already been evacuated. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your state of mind was that the army, and in particular the SVB, was going to investigate what had happened in Grabovica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I use that term very generally, the term "what had happened," because at that stage it just wasn't known the full magnitude of what had happened; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And you knew, because -- well, for a number of reasons -- I'll put a couple of propositions to you. You knew you were obliged to offer assistance to the army -- to the SVB, the army security, in their investigation because your minister, Bakir Alispahic, had told you so the night before; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also knew that taking a purely theoretical view of this, a purely legal and theoretical view, you were obliged in any event to take steps because civilians were among the victims; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us where Mr. Alispahic slept on the night of the 9th of September, incidentally, after his telephone call that you've told us about?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was only one hotel really operating in Jablanica at that time, wasn't there? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that -- what was the name of that particular hotel?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Jablanica Hotel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at that time, a number of rooms were made available for army and government persons; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But also some refugees and expelled people were staying there too; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I've just -- I'll return to what I was asking about, and that was that you had acknowledged that you -- you knew that your organisation was obliged to offer help, and I put to you two bases for that, namely, the instructions of Alispahic, and your legal obligation, viewed from a strictly legal point of view. On the 10th of September, Namik Dzankovic came to your police station, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he was an operative of the SVB, the military security service of the Bosnian army; correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And if there's one thing that's as plain as possible in -- in this case, the SVB of the army was fully competent and indeed fully obliged to investigate crimes by army personnel and, in particular, the crimes at Grabovica. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's right, but I think you should consult military experts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have and we will, but I'm just asking for your comment because you were there. All right. Now, when Mr. Dzankovic came along, he asked for information concerning what had happened in Grabovica and -- and your police station -- or sorry, perhaps I take that back. He asked for information and your police gave him information, as far as you were able to help; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I just want to ask you a question about this. You've been involved in a lot of investigations over time of criminal matters; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it up until -- up until that time though you hadn't been involved in any way in an investigation of a senseless killing of many defenceless and elderly Croatian people; is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that -- all right. I'll take a step back from that now. As far as the criminal process -- as far as the investigative process goes, when you start an investigation, the first thing you do is to collect as much information as you can; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And every investigation is different and unique because of the facts of each case. Is that your experience?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And each investigation has got to take account of the realities that apply on the terrain; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The textbook and theoretical way to conduct an investigation is that you identify the perpetrators; you arrest those perpetrators; you take statements from the perpetrators, from the witnesses; you gather evidence from the terrain; and you place it all in the hands of military prosecutors -- well, sorry, not necessarily military prosecutors but prosecuting authorities, and you let the criminal procedure take its proper course. That's how it should be in theory; correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it's not so easy when you've got members of the 9th Brigade heavily armed and about to go into combat in a major and important operation on the terrain where the crimes took place; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But, however, there was one part of the pre-criminal phase that you could help with, and that was the providing of information. And you did help with that part, didn't you? Because you gave Dzankovic information as and when he asked for it. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there's another part of the -- and an important part of the pre-criminal phase of the investigation, and that is the taking of statements from witnesses. Now, I just want to ask you about this. To your knowledge, did your deputy, Mr. Salihamidzic, take a statement from an eyewitness, Ivan Pranjic?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was a perfectly proper and sensible thing for him to do as an experienced police officer; correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did Mr. Salihamidzic also take a statement from a hydroelectric worker named Alija Turkic?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I just want to clarify this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He conducted an interview with them, a talk, and he tried to get as many facts as possible about what happened, what they heard, what they knew. And then he put all that into a report, an official note, which you have. This is in the case of both of the civilians. Just the basic things were done. They were not on the site. They didn't see the killings. But their information came from different sources.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. But even though they were not on the site and didn't witness the killings, it was still very important for Mr. Salihamidzic, as a professional police officer, to approach them and -- and get such information as they were able to give; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did the police also speak to a -- an individual named Osman Kovacevic, another person who had an association with the hydroelectric plant?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of -- just excuse me a moment. Sorry. I've got -- I've got some other activities that I want to put to you, but I'll come to those in a moment. I'll just try to keep this as chronological as I can. To the best of your recollection, were these statements taken by Salihamidzic on the 10th of September?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, I asked you earlier on about the visit of Namik Dzankovic on the 10th of September. He visited the police station on several occasions over the following fortnight; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how many times he came. It's possible. If you say that it was several occasions, then it's possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And did the police - Mr. Salihamidzic in particular, but you can tell us if any other police did anything also - did they make contact with an officer named Semsudin Halebic to assist with the investigation?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Semsudin Halebic was not a police officer. He was in the military, in the 44th Brigade. I don't know if he held any rank. I don't think that he did. He wasn't a security officer. He worked in the command on some duties, in some service there. Yes, he did conduct an interview with him, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And it was really so -- sorry, just to be -- I understand what you say about that. It was really for that reason I asked you earlier on about the TO Staff. And does that -- did Mr. Halebic have any association with the TO, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know at that point in time whether he was in the 44th Brigade or if he was in the staff headquarters. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. At all events, what you confirm is that Mr. Salihamidzic spoke to him and interviewed him with respect to this matter; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, remaining on the 10th of September. I'm going to come to some other interviews or attempted interviews a bit later on. But on the 10th of September, did Zuka, Zulfikar Alispago, and Edib Saric arrive at the police station and provide certain information to you?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And included in that information that Zulfikar had to disclose was that he had at some stage earlier observed some bodies during his time on the terrain in and near Grabovica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He also provided you with numbers of persons evacuated from the village of Grabovica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, he provided you with another piece of information, that is, that one of his own soldiers had been murdered.

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he was very angry and upset about the murder of one of his own soldiers who was, in fact, an ethnic Croat; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and angry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And did he tell you that the name of that soldier was Ivica Karlovic?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you whether Ivica Karlovic was a good soldier or not?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And Zulfikar also told you that he himself had compiled a report to be sent to the General Staff in Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he ever go so far as to show you that report?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever seen the report?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Incidentally, during the day of the 10th of September, did you hear -- have any communication back from Minister Alispahic concerning any decision or any news at all - I withdraw the term "decision" - I'll ask you the question again. Did Minister Alispahic contact you during the day of the 10th and advise you of the outcome of any discussion that he had with Sefer Halilovic back in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. We're moving slowly through the day of the 10th of September, and I'm grateful to you for keeping concentrating on these matters. Late -- later in the evening on the 10th of September, did you become aware that Zulfikar Alispago had invited Mr. Salihamidzic, Mr. Dzankovic, and Mr. Brankovic to his flat to discuss events in Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Dzankovic and Mr. Salihamidzic and Mr. Brankovic were at my office first, and we called him first, and then he invited them to come to him for a talk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. And you didn't -- you personally were not at that meeting; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've seen though the accounts given of that meeting by -- in reports by Mr. Brankovic and by Mr. Salihamidzic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this court we've seen also an account from Namik Dzankovic, but at the time did you see that Dzankovic report as well or not?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As to those two reports, the report compiled by -- by Salihamidzic was a report to go to you, as chief of the station; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The report compiled by Brankovic was a report to go back to the CSB at Mostar and also to the institution at Konjic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I won't trouble you with their accounts of what happened there, but at all events they told you pretty much straight away what had occurred, because it was quite troubling news, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The news that you had from that meeting was that Ramiz Delalic was claiming to have shot one of his own soldiers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Well, if it's in the report by -- by Salihamidzic, you'd accept that that was the account given to you on the night; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it's in the report, then I would accept it, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Look, I won't march you through every point that's in that report, but you came to know that there was a real danger that Ramiz Delalic would take his troops and go back to Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. But these are military matters that were of no interest to me at that point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I understand that you -- that it was outside of your responsibility. But as a Bosniak, you did have a -- as a member of -- as a Bosnian citizen, I should say, not as a Bosniak -- as a Bosnian citizen generally, you were hoping for a good outcome for the military operation because of the sufferings of the civilians in Mostar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I hear what you say, that you weren't directly involved in the -- in the planning of the combat activities. Very well. I now move to the -- to the 11th of September. Now, I suggest to you that the same process that you'd been engaged in before continued; namely, that you gathered information through whatever sources you could about this incident, and you shared that information with the military security people that you understood were -- were involved in investigating it. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you come to know that there was a rumour or a fear that there was a sniper posted somewhere near the village of Grabovica who posed a possible threat to any investigators?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall that on or about on this date that the news came that troops from Grabovica and also some troops from Jablanica were departing for the battlefield down south near to Dreznica and Vrdi?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were military matters, and I really have no information about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, no, I understand you can't give us any -- any expert or in-depth comment. But as far as the investigation into these crimes goes, you came to know that the troops on the ground from Grabovica were in the process of moving down to Dreznica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me about military matters again, which were not of much interest to me then, because I was a police officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, is that your account, that you just had to interest in the movements of troops from Grabovica, because your role was different?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, although you were not directly involved in military matters at all, you knew that the troops that were stationed in Grabovica were heavily armed and prepared for combat in the area of Dreznica and Vrdi; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And according to your limited knowledge of these matters, you knew that they were good fighters; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know what kind of fighters they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In any event, it was obvious to you and it was a matter of significant concern to you that any attempt to arrest -- well, I withdraw that. Perhaps I should -- I'll take a step back from that. Did you have the name - and I'm talking now about on the 11th of the 9th, or indeed in the days before - did you have the name of a single perpetrator?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just for interest's sake, do you have the name of a single perpetrator now?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have the name of a person who was said to be a soldier who was standing nearby when any such thing happened?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't have any person that you could lawfully arrest at that point. That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to come to the realities of barging into the 9th Brigade and seeking to arrest people. But at this stage in the proceedings, without any identified suspects and without any identified eyewitnesses, to your knowledge, you would not have been entitled to go in and arrest anyone; isn't that accurate?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And leaving aside that question of -- of identified suspects and so on, the fact is it was apparent to you at the time that any attempt to forcibly intervene in the village of Grabovica presented a genuine danger of an armed conflict erupting right there and then; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please simplify your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll do my best. As you sat in your police station in Jablanica, it was apparent to you that if military police or civilian police were sent in to Grabovica to forcibly deal with the situation there, there was a genuine and real prospect of an armed conflict with the units already there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in terms of the realities of sending an armed force into Grabovica, as some might be attempting to suggest elsewhere, how did you get into -- just from your own knowledge, how does one get into the right bank of Grabovica? What's the way in?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you thinking of the geographical aspect --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- or the security aspect?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm thinking of the geographical aspect.

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the entrance to Grabovica, there is a bridge over the Neretva River which larger vehicles could also use to cross, so access was possible to the right bank without any problems, up until the place where there was some military limitations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, okay. But although I understand you're not a military man, that iron bridge would have been relatively easy to defend against an attack to cross it, if anyone wanted to defend that iron bridge; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are, again, some military matters. I would not really like to go into that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Well, look, you've told me a number of times. I'll stop pestering you about it. Thank you, Mr. -- Mr. Zebic. Okay. Well, apart from those matters that I've put to you, I've got another one to ask you about, in terms of investigation. The -- the peacetime situation concerning pathological examination of -- of deceased people, when you were running the civilian police station in peacetime, whereabouts did you used to send a -- a body for a pathologist's examination?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In peacetimes, this was done at hospital facilities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At this stage, was there a pathologist at the hospital in Jablanica? And I mean now in September of 1993.

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that there was no specialist for pathology amongst the doctors at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where the nearest pathologist was?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Sarajevo, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you just explain to the Tribunal how you would have gone about organising the transport of 30 deceased bodies to Sarajevo at that time, if it was up to you to do that. What would you have done and how would you have got them there? Or is there a very short answer to that question, and that is, it wasn't feasible?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You've given the right answer. It wasn't feasible. It wasn't possible at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks very much. I want to take you on to the 12th of -- of September now. You indicated that you were told by an officer, Senad Dzino, that he -- sorry, pardon me. I'll take a step back. On the 12th of -- on the 12th of September, the War Presidency was concerned to find out what was happening, in terms of the investigation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And speaking from the military side, Senad Dzino, who was the deputy commander of the 44th Brigade, the local Jablanica brigade, gave you some news about that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to me but to the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. Very well. And then you indicated yesterday that -- that the news he gave was that he understood that Sefer Halilovic and -- and Vehbija Karic had indicated that the army was going to investigate this matter; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Senad Dzino, he wasn't an SVB operative, was he? He wasn't from the military security. He was an actual combat commander in the normal line of military commander. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was the deputy commander of the 44th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. In the following days -- sorry, pardon me. But the -- but the SVB commander from that -- sorry, the SVB operative from the 44th Brigade was, in fact, a man called Sihirlic Zajko; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. In this trial, we've had tendered into evidence a document emanating from Mr. Eminovic of the 6th Corps SVB which asks -- which is directed to Zajko and to Dzankovic, and I wanted to ask you this question: To your knowledge, Zajko Sihirlic did continue to help Mr. Dzankovic in his tasks in the following week; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. I assume so, because the colleagues from the service were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. We also have -- have heard evidence from Mr. Eminovic, and he says that he gave certain tasks to the military police in the days following the killings of -- the killings at Grabovica. Are you able to comment on whether that happened or not, whether -- whether you know about what tasks Eminovic gave to the military police in that time?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. He did not forward a copy of that order to the police station, no request for cooperation or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that. And was -- and just in terms of the normal practice, there was no need for Eminovic to send copies of letters to you, was there?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I understand. Okay. Well, I won't -- I take it this is the case -- I'll ask you a general question. It might cut short a long list of other questions. But you can't comment really on what correspondence passed between Eminovic and the local military police or local SVB bodies; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I won't ask you about them. But there is one other matter I want to ask you about concerning that, and that is Mr. Brankovic. Now, to your knowledge, Mr. Brankovic was very often in the company of Mr. Dzankovic and was helping him during the fortnight, the two weeks, following the killings at Grabovica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those two seemed to have -- I just ask for your comment about this, actually. But as far as you could see, those two seemed to have quite a good working relationship?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And to your knowledge, Brankovic was a professional and very thorough officer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Did Brankovic have access to a vehicle at that time? Let me ask the question another way: Did Brankovic sometimes have access to a vehicle at that time?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the petrol situation applying to the use of petrol for police vehicles?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Petrol was in short supply, but whenever we had petrol, we helped him out so that he should be able to go out on his missions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. And was it a -- was it a day-to-day question whether there was any petrol available to go out on the terrain at that time?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember that it was that dire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. When was it that you would -- can you just explain how -- how the petrol situation operated. Did you have your own petrol dump at the police station?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you go to get the fuel when you needed it?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our main supply was the petrol station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. And did you have any -- did you, as the police force, have any priority over normal civilians, in terms of access to petrol?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had priority over civilians. However, the army had priority over us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. That was my next question, but -- very well. I understand that. And did there have to be a special requisition form to get petrol, or did you just go there and take your chance?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The supply of petrol that the War Presidency was in charge would be distributed among the three components: According to needs, according to availability, so that everybody would get their share at the petrol station as it was allocated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I think perhaps my questions there were coming from a background of someone from a market economy completely. Was the distribution of petrol regulated from a high level, or was it just market forces at work at the petrol station?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said the War Presidency decided, because the War Presidency was in charge of all the supplies of everything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I do understand your answer. Okay. We have heard evidence in this court -- or perhaps I should ask you this: Throughout this time, when you were making -- when you were doing what you could to help the investigation, to your knowledge did the -- the shells continue to fall on Jablanica from time to time?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult to remember from this distance, but it is a fact that Jablanica was constantly under fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Very well. Now, doing the best you can -- I understand what you've said about the military, your -- that you weren't connected to the military operations in any way. We've heard evidence in this court from a previous witness that the combat operations commenced on or about the 13th of September and that there was combat activity pretty much straight through until about the 20th of September, when some of the Sarajevo units or all of the Sarajevo units were pulled out and went home. I want to ask you, first of all: Did you become aware that there was combat after the 13th of -- of September on a wide front from Crni Vrh, up in the north, right down to Vrdi, in the south?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't obtain that information officially. I heard it from the news, from the radio, and television and -- and newspapers, ask the news travelled fast among people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. And apart from that combat activity that you heard about in the way you've just described, did you -- did it come to your attention that the Sarajevo units were passing through Jablanica on their way back to -- back to Sarajevo on or about the 20th of -- of September?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody drew my attention to that in particular. I just knew that they were on their way to Sarajevo, pulling out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. And did you actually see any of the trucks driving through Jablanica on their way?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could be. But I didn't pay attention.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you've given some information about activities undertaken by police officers and in particular about Mr. Salihamidzic and statements that he took from people. I just want to ask you now about some operative information that may have come your way and see whether you became aware of these steps. You knew an individual named Dzelmo who you said was from the military -- I think you said the military police. But I'll just clarify that. You knew Mr. Dzelmo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are several of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dzenaid Dzelmo is the one I'm talking about. Do you know him?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you become aware -- now, he's not a -- he's not a civilian policeman, is he?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But nevertheless, in the exchange of information that you had with -- with Namik Dzankovic from time to time and indeed Sead Brankovic, did it come to your knowledge that Delmo -- Dzelmo, I'm sorry, had been to Grabovica and attempted to speak to the citizens and refugees there on the left bank of Grabovica but they had been too scared to give him -- to talk to him or to give any statements?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I understand -- this is sort of -- this is 11 years distance now and some of these details may be hard to recall, but that was certainly part of your knowledge at the time that attempts had been made to speak to the -- the refugees who were living in Grabovica but that those refugees had not cooperated, whatever the reason may be. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I suggest to you that similar information -- similar operative information came to you that Nusret Sahic -- could you please just explain to the Court who Nusret Sahic is? Or was, more accurately.

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know -- did you know the man Nusret Sahic who had an association with military police in Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand you at first the way you pronounced the name. You mean Nusret Sahic? I know him. He was a Military Police Battalion commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You must forgive the Australian mispronunciation, Mr. Zebic. I apologise for it. That is the individual I'm talking about. Did you come to know that he, too, had tried to speak to refugees and, in fact, that he had succeeded in speaking to one individual called Muharem, a man called Muharem, who was a Muslim refugee?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible that he told me, but I'd forgotten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does it ring a bell now -- or does it assist your memory for me to say this name, Muharem? Do you recall being told about that individual? Who was said to be a -- a Muslim refugee on the -- living on the left bank after the evacuation of the Croat civilians?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm just about to move to another topic now. I'm in the Court's hands. I, from my own point of view, would be happy if there was a short break, because of pains in the legs, quite frankly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. And could you tell me how long do you still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: 20 minutes. Yes. Let us take a break, you know. We'll resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Morrissey. Try to finish your cross-examination in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I will. Could the witness please be shown MFI277. Your Honours, I'm hearing the Bosnian. Just a moment. I know the problem. Your Honours, it was my problem. Not anyone else's. It's now fixed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Pardon me, Mr. Zebic. I apologise for all that. Do you have in front of you that order that you gave? Sorry, when I say "that order," that note that you sent. I withdraw that.

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Okay. Now, the second paragraph is the one I wanted to ask you about here. In particular, there's a sentence there where -- where you say: "We feel it is necessary that you secure conditions for carrying out complete clearing up of the terrain and performing complete on-site investigation." You then go on to clarify that by saying: "Or, in other words, establishing necessary facts about the event in which people whose bodies were being buried had been killed." Now, can I just ask you this: What did you mean by saying "securing the conditions for carrying out complete clearing up of the terrain and performing complete on-site investigation"?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document was written on the 29th September, that is, 20 days after the event we discussed. You see it was written - and you see that from the first paragraph - based on information that the public security station received from citizens and troops. We had been informed that there were still corpses there that hadn't been buried and that the stench was pervasive, and I thought, therefore, that it was my duty to initiate through the command of the 44th Mountain Brigade some sort of action to try to clarify the incident, at least based on the remaining clues.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, who were you contemplating would do that inspection once the conditions were secured for doing it?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be the task of a technical service, such as on the level of the ministry in Sarajevo or the Security Services Centre in Sarajevo, down to our level, such as providing a pathologist to perform post-mortems, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, first of all, in -- in general terms, the persons who were to do the on-site inspection that's mentioned in that report, did you envisage those persons to come from the MUP, from the Ministry of the Interior, or from the military?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My letter, as I said, was a repeated urging. Everything else was pure operative work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I understand that, and I understand also that you're not giving orders, but I just need to clarify -- I just need to clarify this issue -- sorry, pardon me, Mr. Zebic. I'm just trying to change what I can see on the screen. I need to clarify from you -- I understand what you say about the letter, but I press you for an answer about this. You were talking about an on-site investigation by the Ministry of the Interior, whether at the Sarajevo level or at -- or including -- no, that question just got mired down. I withdraw it. I'm sorry. You had in mind Ministry of the Interior investigators there, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you indicated yesterday that your centre had certain technical resources. You mentioned cameras and certain testing kits and so on. But it still remains the fact, doesn't it, that in order to deal with the massacre of a whole village, as it began to appear and as it now begins to appear, you needed more resources than what the relatively small Jablanica police station had available; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For this to be -- for a proper on-site investigation to take place, what was needed was support at the highest level from the MUP in Sarajevo to provide pathologists and other crime scene staff and resources; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And quite frankly, Mr. Zebic, you had plenty of other work for your crime scene people to do in the Jablanica municipality at that time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. The last document I want to show you now is MFI222.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to show you now, Mr. Zebic - and this is the last of the documents that you're to be shown by me in all events - this is the Brankovic letter which you referred to earlier on that you'd seen and which you understood he was submitting to superiors in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, would it be possible, please, to go to the second page of the English version of that document, so the following page.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you just take the opportunity to look at that document again and -- and just reassure yourself that that is the Brankovic report which --

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let me -- I have to ask you the questions formally, first of all. Is that the Brankovic report that you referred to in evidence earlier on that was directed to Alica Bilic and to another person called Nedzad Surkovic in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I -- I understand that in some respects you know what you were told here, but I'm just going to take you through some aspects of this document, if you don't mind. First of all, Brankovic says in the first paragraph that: "The attitude of the civilian authorities of Jablanica municipality and the Bosnian army's conduct towards the inhabitants was correct. They were given humanitarian aid. They received medical air. And except for some sporadic attacks on Croatian property, no incidents took place which could have related in the persecution of the inhabitants or which could have caused them to leave. As far as we knew, 33 Croatians lived in the village." Now, as far as you knew, that information was perfectly accurate; correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, just excuse me for one moment, please. I'm sorry, Mr. Zebic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I just want to be sure that we've got the right document in front of you there. Could I just ask you, Mr. Zebic: The document in front of you, does it end with a paragraph saying that: "On the 11th of September, 1993, the Sefer Halilovic, the Chief of Staff, appealed to me and to Namik Dzankovic." I just want to make sure that you haven't been given the Salihamidzic report by mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And there's no criticism of the court staff, but I just know that when we provided this document we did so in a way that was just a little bit difficult to navigate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you mind -- do you have in front of you the last page of that document? You'll have to -- if you need it to be scrolled, just say so, and the court staff will do that for you.

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the first page in front of me. I still have the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could it be possible for the witness to have the second page of the document, please.

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right. This is the report -- or rather, the official note by Mr. Salihamidzic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's all right now. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Do you now have the -- the Brankovic report in front of you?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the first page.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Yes. Excellent. Very well. Okay. I'll just continue with that now. Does it -- does the document -- well, sorry, the document goes on to say that -- the document goes on to give certain details of the visit of your deputy, Salihamidzic. And then it gives the account that "When the deputy chief of the Jablanica police station and leader" -- I'm reading now from the bottom of the -- the second paragraph. "When the deputy chief of the Jablanica police station and leader of the Jablanica military police company arrived at the spot where Marinko Maric's body was to be -- was supposed to be, Ramiz Delalic, also known as Celo, approached them, and then asked 'Have you found anything? While you're busy searching for them, look what they're doing to us.' Probably referring to the detainees of the Dretelj camp who were in the village of Grabovica on the left bank of the River Neretva." Now, does that account given by Brankovic in this letter, is that the same account that you were given by Salihamidzic when he came back on the actual day that he made that village -- visit to the village?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the same description.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, did this report contain a reference to "the Karic story," namely --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, could the witness be shown the second page, please. And I'm also on the second page now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You may find this a little difficult to -- to see, and we may have to focus in some way. I'm -- I just want to take you to a part here though about Karic. This report says that "Ramiz Delalic" -- this is the Brankovic report, it says: "Ramiz Delalic, also known as Celo, came in. He was obviously excited. He was accompanied by his deputy whose name was Malco. He said that he had just executed one of his soldiers and threatened to withdraw his units back to Sarajevo and said that he did not care about Mostar. He cursed Minister Bakir Alispahic and his Laste Unit and said that the MUP members were masquerading like dummies, that they were no good at fighters and that they should be sent to Mostar. He said that he had asked Vehbija Karic what he should do if the Croats refused to let them move into the houses, to which Vehbija Karic allegedly responded, 'Kill them and throw them into the lake," and that his men had understood this literally and that as a result the crime had been committed." Now, is that account that we find in Brankovic's report here the same thing that you were told by Salihamidzic when he came back from the meeting -- let me just ask that question again. I've got two people confused. Is that report that I've just read out to you there from Brankovic, is that the same thing that Brankovic told you when they came back from the flat having supposedly seen Ramiz Delalic, Celo, and had that conversation?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My deputy told me that when they came back. You were asking whether Mr. Brankovic told me. My deputy told me that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Okay. I understand. When your deputy told you that, was Mr. Brankovic present or not?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Brankovic was together with my deputy at Mr. Alispago's when this happened and when this was said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Very well. And Brankovic finally says that: "On the 11th of September, 1993 Sefer Halilovic, the Chief of Staff, appealed to me and Namik Dzankovic. He insisted that an investigation be conducted to establish the facts. He said that he never had nor ever would condone the crimes committed." Now, this is what Brankovic put in the report that you saw. Did Brankovic tell you about that before you saw this report? Did he tell you what Sefer Halilovic's position was before you saw this report?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did. What's written here confirms what he actually told me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. All right. Are you able to recall -- although the date here says the 11th of September, 1993, I'd ask you to just exercise an independent memory, if you can, about that. Are you able to recall, when it was that Brankovic passed this information on to you, or is it too long ago to remember?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember where you were when he passed that information on to you?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my office in the public security station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. Okay. And -- well, you've already indicated your view of his professionalism. Okay. There's just --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I -- this document has been tendered, but you'll recall there was some discussion about it because I showed it to witnesses who hadn't seen it before. They'd heard of it, but they hadn't seen it. In order to make sure of it, I now seek to complete, so to say, the tendering of this exhibit, MFI222. I apologise, too, to the Prosecution and the Court because we -- by an error, we mixed the two documents in together. Now they've both been fully acknowledged, I just seek to tender it as one exhibit. We can divide it if we have to, but I'll be guided by the Prosecutors, actually, about that. If they wish to divide it, actually we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: There's no objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe that document was used by you first. Right?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: For this witness, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: But I understand it was used by the Defence earlier on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Through another witness, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. But anyway, we have it admitted into the evidence, and it doesn't matter whose document it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. And -- I must acknowledge that the confusion that arose about it was mine entirely. I apologise for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: All right -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zebic, I promised 20 minutes. I've gone two minutes over. But I'm just going to ask two minutes of questions now, with -- with the Court's leave, and then I'm finished now. The last series of questions is this, and they concern Mr. Alispahic's arrival in Jablanica. I have asked you questions about this before, and you've given some answers. When Alispahic arrived, in whose -- who was he in the company of?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I talked to him in my office, but I don't know who came with him to Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was providing security for the Minister of the Interior when he arrived in Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Probably somebody from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who provided him with a vehicle to get from -- to get down the hill into Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that either, but it was the practice for us to send a vehicle from our station to Glogosnica, where we had a reserve station, and that's where we would bring our associates back from, those who were coming back from Mostar to Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've given evidence that you don't know where he stayed. What were the options, in terms of accommodation, in Jablanica at that time for a minister -- in fact, for a minister of the high importance and standing of Minister Bakir Alispahic?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You yourself said that the hotel was the only place where people could be accommodated, so it's possible that he slept at the hotel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there anyone else apart from yourself at the police station who you'd expect to be notified of where the Minister of the Interior was staying when he came to your town?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. Perhaps he told me. I don't remember. Maybe at the moment I just cannot remember where that was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And finally, in the event that a minister had to go from Jablanica to Konjic the following day, where would that minister procure a vehicle in Jablanica in order to get from Jablanica to Konjic? And I've used the word "minister." What I really mean is: Where would Bakir Alispahic get a vehicle?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be the best that it's a vehicle from the public security station, but it's possible that also the army would provide a vehicle for him to Konjic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know how relations were between Bakir Alispahic and the army at that time or not?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zebic, thank you for your patience in answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: That's the end of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any redirect?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva. Re-examined by Mr. Sachdeva:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zebic, in response to a question by my learned friend - and this is, for my learned friend's benefit, on page 47, line 12 - the question was, and I quote: "And apart from saying the word 'Sefer' when he commenced the phone call, this -- Mr. Alispahic didn't use the word 'Sefer' again during that conversation, during that telephone call." And then he goes on to say: "After the telephone call, he didn't mention Sefer again by name, but he just told you, I suggest, you help the military security out when they investigate." And he asked you if that's correct. And your answer was: "Sounds about right." Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, yesterday I asked you with respect to that conversation: "When the conversation ended, what did Mr. Alispahic say?" And you answered to me: "He said that he had spoken to Mr. Halilovic, that they had agreed -- or rather, they had received a promise that the case would be investigated. He gave me oral orders that if any assistance was required from the Jablanica Public Security Station and the police service, that we should provide any such assistance to the military security services." Do you recall that answer?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you can, can you please, for the Court's benefit, explain or clarify your answer or explain the inconsistency.

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that, in my opinion, there were no inconsistencies. Perhaps the question by the Defence counsel was a little long so I had lost my thread. I think that's the only thing here. After the conversation was finished, Mr. Bakir told me that he had spoken with Mr. Sefer and that he promised him what I said in my statement, that steps would be taken for the case to be investigated, and after that, if required, we should provide assistance. This is what I said, so I stand by that part of the statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to be clear, Mr. Zebic, your answer to me yesterday was, "He had spoken to Mr. Halilovic," and now you say "Sefer." If you can, can you clarify that, please.

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Bosnia and Herzegovina, there's a name -- the first name and the last name. In this case, the first name is Sefer; the last name is Halilovic. So in this instance, we are talking about Mr. Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You were also asked by counsel for the Defence about the availability of a pathologist with respect to any investigation that could have been conducted in Grabovica. Do you know whether a pathologist would have been available to come up from Sarajevo to conduct an investigation at that time?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many people left Sarajevo, even in the most difficult circumstances. And had anyone requested it and organised it and felt it was necessary, a pathologist would be able to leave Sarajevo too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware whether the ABiH, that is, the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, had any pathologists available to investigate the murder of civilians at that time? And if you do know that, where would they be located?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if there were any or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were also asked by counsel for the Defence whether you were aware of -- whether Sefer Halilovic was the subject of surveillance by the Ministry of the Interior or the Ministry of -- by the security service in Sarajevo. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would there be any reason for Mr. Alispahic to let you know, chief of police, civilian police in Jablanica, whether there was any surveillance on Mr. Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Morrissey also asked you about the resources you had with respect to any investigation. Are you aware whether the ABiH had inferior or superior resources compared to your police station to do any investigation of civilian killings?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry, I'll just have to intervene. I didn't ask that question. The comparative merits of one as against another doesn't arise out of cross-examining, so it's, in my submission, not something that can arise in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Morrissey has asked this witness plenty of questions with respect to the resources or not of the -- of the police station to conduct an investigation in Grabovica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, you may ask a direct question without comparison with the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether the ABiH had a -- had resources or not to do any investigation?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Morrissey also asked you about whether you would have been entitled to go into Grabovica and arrest anyone there. Do you recall being asked that?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you as a civilian police officer have the authority to go into Grabovica and arrest military personnel for crimes committed against civilians?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Lastly, Mr. Zebic, you recall being asked about a photograph of Mr. Sefer at the police station in Jablanica; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who put that photograph up there?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who took it down?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why the photograph was there?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the start of the aggression on Bosnia and Herzegovina, the name of Mr. Sefer Halilovic was well known to all citizens, especially those who had joined in the defence of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. He appeared in the media and especially you could hear a lot about him through the military structures as one of the highest military authorities at the time, and many accepted him and understood him to be a commander right from the beginning and that is why some of these photographs appeared. You could see them not only in offices but also in public places too. So as far as I'm concerned, it was nothing unusual to find such a photograph on the premises of the public security station in Jablanica. Why it was taken down, what the reasons for that were, probably that came about because of the replacing of Mr. Sefer Halilovic from the post that he had held to date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long was the photograph up there?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: That's the examination -- re-examination, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge El Mahdi. JUDGE EL MAHDI: Thank you, Mr. President. Questioned by the Court: JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Witness, I have a question to put to you. It relates to your testimony when you said that two women came to see you, two Muslim women. And these two women told you about the events that had taken place in Grabovica. Could you confirm the date of this, please.

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This happened in the morning, on the 9th of September, 1993. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] So it is on the 9th. And you also said that on the same day and following this complaint, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I still didn't do anything until the information was confirmed by military personnel. This happened on the same day. Maybe an hour or two after the visit by these young women. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Yes. So you had the feeling that these people must have been from the army, that these people must have been military, and these were responsible for this. It didn't cross your mind that it could have been just anybody. It could have been civilians, for instance.

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Because the young women who originally told us this information said that the original firing was heard in the part where the military units were billeted. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Very well. So you waited until noon approximately, when the commander of the unit called the Igman Wolves came to see you. I believe they were called the Igman Wolves. And it's after that, once he had told you about what had happened, that you started to do something about it.

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] So why did this person turn to you? He could have turned to the military authorities or the military.

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not clear to me to this day why he came to the police instead of going to the higher military command. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Because they thought that you were the people vested with that kind of power.

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Just something else I would like to clarify, please: In the night of the 9th, you saw Mr. Alispahic, who came to see you. Where did this meeting take place? Was it at the police station?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in my office. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] But did this -- before this person came to see you, you were in a building where Mr. Cibo had his office; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Therefore, you went to the police station to -- to receive Mr. Alispahic so that you could meet him there.

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response] JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] My last question: On reading the report by Mr. Brankovic, which contains the following information -- it is stated that he was in charge, as well as Mr. Dzankovic, in charge of conducting the investigations. Mr. Halilovic had given instructions to that effect. And they realised that Mr. Alispahic told you that the police, if necessary, had to take part in these investigations. Now, don't you think -- or do you think that you were the right person to be conducting these investigations?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: None of us asked that a -- an investigation be conducted. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Thank you. [In English] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any questions out of Judge's questions? I see none. At this stage, are there any documents to tender? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's MFI277.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: The Prosecution seeks admission of that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I believe that's -- the Defence used it; right? Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: None whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. It's admitted into the evidence. On the part of Defence, are there documents to tender at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Nothing in addition to what was already done, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, Witness, thank you very much for coming to The Hague to give your evidence. Madam Usher will show you out of the room, and we wish you a pleasant journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re. Any submissions concerning with the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. I have an application I wish to make. Could we move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go into the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, good afternoon -- good evening, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I'm sorry to keep you waiting for so long. We only have about ten minutes to go for this evening. But anyway, would you please make the solemn declaration in accordance with the paper Madam Usher is showing to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we just move into private session for one moment, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that you have to ask some questions about his name to be on the record in open session first. Then we'll go into the private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'll do that. Examined by Mr. Re:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your name is Ahmed Salihamidzic? And you were born on the 24th of July, 1946, and your present occupation is a retired deputy police chief. You're a pensioner. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMED SALIHAMIDZIC
utterances.text: Yes., correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go into the private session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to lead you through some background information, which is probably about as far as we'll get today. From 1974 to 1981, were you a member of the police force in Jablanica and its commander from 1978 to 1981, when you left police work until returning to the Jablanica police station in January 1993?

utterances.speaker: AHMED SALIHAMIDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hold the post of deposit chief and the chief's assistant when you returned in 1993?

utterances.speaker: AHMED SALIHAMIDZIC
utterances.text: My position was deputy head.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the head, of course, was Mr. Zebic, who has just completed his testimony here; correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMED SALIHAMIDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you, in fact, retired from that position in April 1998.

utterances.speaker: AHMED SALIHAMIDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's go straight to the 9th of September, 1993. Were you working at the Jablanica police station on that day?

utterances.speaker: AHMED SALIHAMIDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Mr. Zebic also working on that day?

utterances.speaker: AHMED SALIHAMIDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Zebic speak to you about something that had happened, or did you speak to him about something that had happened?

utterances.speaker: AHMED SALIHAMIDZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zebic called me into his office and Saric Edib was there at the time with this deputy. We exchanged some information on that occasion regarding events in Grabovica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know someone called Edib Saric?

utterances.speaker: AHMED SALIHAMIDZIC
utterances.text: I didn't know him until then. He had come then to the police station to see the chief. The chief summoned me, and that's when I met him for the first time, him and his deputy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you exchanged some information on that occasion regarding events in Grabovica. What was the information about the events in Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: AHMED SALIHAMIDZIC
utterances.text: Right. The chief stated that on that day, the 9th, two girls had come to the police station to report that on the right bank of the Neretva in the settlement of Grabovica there was shooting which was upsetting the civilians, Croat civilians, who inhabited Grabovica. He suggested that we go to Grabovica to check that information. Mr. Edib Saric confirmed that. I insisted, in view of the fact that they had said army troops had arrived in Sarajevo, I insisted that somebody from the military come along, specifically the military police commander of the 44th Brigade, and Mr. Saric agreed, and we went together to inspect or to investigate on site in a police vehicle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Salihamidzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, now is the time for the break. Witness, as I did to other witnesses in this Tribunal, I have to warn you that now you are under the oath, so do not talk to anybody about your testimony and do not let anybody talk to you about it. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I hope you have a good rest, and I'll see you tomorrow morning at 9.00 in the same courtroom. The hearing for today is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 18th day of March, 2005, at 9.00 a.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
